title: Justice Needs and Satisfaction in the United States of America — Legal Problems in Daily Life

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess AI’s jagged capabilities, verification needs or human–AI deployment directly. Instead, it redirects attention toward people-centred justice outcomes, task unbundling, differentiated provider roles and continuously evaluated, scalable service design—an operating-model perspective relevant to the cluster but grounded in legal-needs evidence rather than AI performance.

st.t: Justice gap: Fair resolution exceeds legal assistance
st.an: The source directly endorses the cluster’s broad, outcome-focused conception of access to justice and materially develops it by operationalising a respondent-assessed fair-resolution gap across civil and criminal problems and all income groups. It also advances a people-centred reform agenda based on evidence, prevention, innovation and services beyond courts and law firms, while qualifying its national extrapolations as indicative.

kp.k: People-centered evidence provides a baseline for justice reform
kp.d: IAALS and HiiL investigate access to fair resolution rather than AI adoption. Their survey collected 10,058 adult observations in August and September 2020 through IPSOS’ probability-recruited Knowledge Panel, asking about legal problems experienced over the preceding four years. Population weights were used for prevalence and distribution analyses, but subsequent analyses of the most serious problems were unweighted. Findings concern respondents’ experiences and perceptions, not independently adjudicated measures of fairness.

All responses were completed
We call it people-centered justice.

kp.k: Legal needs extend across the income spectrum
kp.d: The report finds that 66% of Americans experienced at least one legal problem over four years and 49% of reported problems were completely resolved. Problem prevalence did not differ significantly by household income, although problem types, seriousness and resolution differed. The authors argue that reform must address broad societal demand rather than focus exclusively on low-income people’s access to lawyers.

kp.k: Annual justice-gap estimates depend on broad extrapolation assumptions
kp.d: The authors estimate 260 million legal problems annually and a justice resolution gap of 120 million problems. Their calculation combines problems with no expected future resolution and unfairly resolved problems; 29% had no resolution expected, while 17% of completely resolved problems were reported unfair or very unfair. Annualization divides the four-year observations by three rather than four to compensate for forgotten encounters. The report explicitly treats the estimate as indicative and assumption-dependent, rather than a direct annual count.

kp.k: Disadvantage concerns seriousness and resolution, not just prevalence
kp.d: Lower-income respondents experienced more serious problems and lower resolution rates. Women reported higher average seriousness than men, 6.17 versus 5.60, and disproportionately experienced domestic violence and abuse. Multiracial and Black respondents reported particularly high prevalence, 74% and 71%; Black respondents reported the highest average seriousness, 6.51. The authors recommend prioritizing vulnerable groups while recognizing different patterns across income, gender, race, age and location.

kp.k: Justice needs encompass emotional, financial and relational harms
kp.d: Forty-four percent of respondents with legal problems reported negative consequences from their most serious problem. The report distinguishes these harms from the stress, money and time spent pursuing resolution. Employment, domestic violence, family and public-benefits problems rank highly on its impact measure. The authors recommend services that address psychological and relational consequences alongside legal and financial needs, rather than equating resolution with winning a legal proceeding.

kp.k: Resolution involves diverse formal and informal providers
kp.d: The dataset contains more than 820 combinations of sources of help. Among people involving at least one source, respondents used 1.9 sources on average, or 2.2 including direct negotiation. Lawyers and family members were the most common sources, at 23% and 21%, while courts accounted for 14%. Insurance companies, financial institutions, medical professionals and mental health professionals also played substantial roles. The authors oppose assuming a single lawyer-to-court pathway and suggest integrated services for complex problems.

kp.k: Provider ratings differ between process quality and outcomes
kp.d: Medical and mental health professionals and lawyers generally received high procedural-quality ratings; courts, employers and government agencies generally scored lower. Insurance companies, financial institutions and local agencies performed relatively well on distributive outcomes. These comparisons concern perceived service quality and differing problem mixes, not proof of causal provider superiority. The report acknowledges courts’ mandated neutrality, statutory restrictions and more complicated disputes, while recommending procedural improvements and learning from healthcare providers.

kp.k: Complete resolution often leaves harms inadequately repaired
kp.d: The report distinguishes distributive justice from restoration of damage. Fewer than 17% agreed that outcomes repaired relational harm, fewer than 15% that they restored lost time, and fewer than 30% of those losing money that their justice journey restored it. Lawyers and courts received low ratings for damage restoration. The authors advocate stronger restorative elements in service design, rather than treating case closure as sufficient evidence of successful justice delivery.

kp.k: Discrete interventions suggest opportunities for unbundled services
kp.d: Respondents reported 13,031 interventions across 4,041 most-serious problems involving interventions: averages of 3.2 per problem and 2.5 per source of help. Advice, paperwork and talking to the other party were most common. The report finds no single intervention universally increased complete resolution after controls, but reports an association between more interventions and better resolution outcomes, and model-specific advantages over advice for mediation, decisions, paperwork and representation. It cautions that complete resolution does not necessarily mean greater effectiveness or satisfaction. The authors recommend unbundling simple interventions, reserving comprehensive packages for more complex needs.

kp.k: Online information influences decisions, but differs from resolution
kp.d: Among respondents seeking legal information or advice, the internet was the most frequently reported resource, 31%, followed by lawyers, 29%. Among internet users, 63% said online information affected their resolution decisions; 73% used search engines and 62% specific websites. These findings concern information-seeking, not AI or autonomous legal work. Only 94 online-dispute-resolution interventions were recorded, too few for the report’s intervention comparison. The authors recommend improving online information and integrating online and in-person services.

kp.k: Service demand is not explained by price alone
kp.d: Among those not seeking information or advice from lawyers, 26% considered a lawyer unnecessary and 14% cited inability to afford one; other explanations included believing the issue was not legal or appropriate for a lawyer. Emotional support was the most frequently reported information-and-advice assistance, 52%. Respondents valued trustworthiness, 46%, ease of understanding, 39%, situation-specific guidance, 31%, and professional provenance, 31%, above delivery mode. The authors interpret this as demand for broader services and possible willingness to pay for appropriate help, not evidence that affordability is irrelevant.

kp.k: Employment disputes expose limits of workplace-centered resolution
kp.d: One-sixth of Americans experienced employment problems over four years. Among respondents identifying employment as their most serious problem, 67% took action, 48% engaged their employer, 32% completely resolved the problem and 52% expected no resolution. Those not acting frequently cited expected futility or the other party’s advantage. The authors suggest employer–employee power imbalances as a possible explanation. Employment problems arising after the pandemic began were frequently attributed to COVID-19, and the authors predict continuing need rather than establishing subsequent outcomes.

kp.k: Debt problems combine high action rates with financial barriers
kp.d: Money-related problems affected approximately one-sixth of Americans. Four-fifths of those identifying such a problem as most serious acted, but 40% completely resolved it and 38% still expected resolution. Abandoned money problems had higher average impact than resolved or ongoing ones, unlike the other problem categories showing significant differences. Lawyers were used by approximately one-third of respondents involving help. The authors connect financial constraints to difficulties pursuing resolution and recommend accessible, low-cost alternative assistance.

kp.k: Scaling justice services requires evidence, investment and regulatory change
kp.d: The authors argue that neither traditional nor nontraditional providers deliver sufficiently consistent, high-quality resolution at population scale. They recommend substantial R&D, evidence-based combinations of interventions, specialization, user-centered design, integration with health and social services, and diagnostic triage. They identify regulation and fragmented delivery as possible constraints on supply and cite Utah and Arizona experimentation as grounds for wider regulatory reform. These are policy recommendations grounded in their interpretation of unmet need, not demonstrated effects of AI or specific regulatory changes.

kp.k: Limitations constrain causal and subgroup interpretations
kp.d: The report identifies possible underreporting of sensitive problems, small subsamples, uncertain household-income comparability, imperfect recall, and difficulties estimating money and time. Immigration findings warrant particular caution because only 64 respondents identified immigration as their most serious problem. The study did not separately investigate hidden communities such as homeless or incarcerated people and excluded children. COVID-19 could not be fully isolated from other influences. The authors call for additional and longitudinal data to evaluate interventions and delivery models.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The report contains no concrete claims or predictions specifically about AI changing legal services.
pts.d: IAALS and HiiL discuss technology, internet-based legal information, online dispute resolution, scalable justice services, and evidence-based reform. They do not identify these technologies as AI or attribute changes in legal services to AI. These broader digital-justice statements should not be recast as AI predictions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.d: The report's survey evidence concerns Americans' legal problems, sources of assistance, justice journeys, perceived outcomes, and use of online information. It does not evaluate an AI system, measure AI adoption or performance, or establish AI's effects on service delivery. The survey therefore provides context about justice needs rather than evidence for an AI-related claim.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: No timeframe or conditions for AI-driven change are stated.
pts.d: The 2021 report draws on a 2020 survey about legal problems experienced over the preceding four years and discusses future justice reform. Those dates frame the justice-needs research, not a prediction about AI. Its expectations concerning increased online justice delivery do not establish an AI-specific forecast.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: No population or professional role is identified as affected specifically by AI.
pts.d: The report addresses the public's unmet justice needs and implications for courts, lawyers, informal and non-traditional sources of assistance, and policymakers. It highlights unequal burdens across demographic and income groups, but does not connect those burdens or proposed improvements to AI. It makes no AI-specific claim about lawyer displacement, staffing, pricing, provider competition, or access to justice.
